items.title: Jerome Richardson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996
items.q: And at times I think that was the trouble sometimes with the Duke Ellington Band. Some of those guys who were in that band who left the band just about couldn’t do anything and didn’t do anything without that framework of Duke Ellington around them.

ctx.x: It’s nice that he has a big band to play in too, because there’s not all the opportunities I guess that there used to be as far as —

Well there are good things to say about big bands and good things to say about small groups. In a small group you have a chance to play on every piece. In a big band, there is no way that everybody can play on a piece, you know, so sometimes there’s one guy, sometimes it’s another and this and that. There are times when you really don’t get a chance to play what you feel in a big band. You don’t have time to play it. Somebody else is doing it. And in that you’re better off in a way playing with a small group,…
Most of them came back to the band, didn’t they?
